newsitem.title: USA: U.S. gas firms, customers see benefits from choice.
newsitem.headline: U.S. gas firms, customers see benefits from choice.

text.p: U.S. natural gas firms and customers are already starting to see benefits from programs that allow smaller commercial and residential accounts to choose their gas supplier, industry sources said this week.
While federal laws in 1993 forced pipelines to unbundle upstream services, only recently have a number of state pilot programs brought some competition to the burner tip.
"Residential unbundling is good for the customer and good for growing our utility business," Joel Singer, president of Bay State Gas Co in Massachusetts, told a gas conference here.
Bay State's Pioneer Valley program, which began in November, offered retail customers a choice of service from 10 marketers and resulted in savings of between five and 10 percent.

Singer said the company hoped to offer choice system-wide by the end of the year, noting competition spurred a number of innovative pricing and marketing techniques that should eventually translate into increased system throughput.

Bay State, New England's largest distribution company (LDC) serving more than 300,000 gas customers in three states, eventually plans to exit the gas merchant function and concentrate instead on transmission.
"It's very inefficient for a utility to stay half in and half out of the merchant business," Singer said, noting the high cost of maintaining dual infrastructures.

As of late last year, there were at least 16 states with residential gas pilot programs or broader customer choice plans, but each scheme is different, with some LDCs opting to compete with marketers for a share of the retail business.

"These pilot programs are R&D (research and development) opportunities. We learned we could deliver gas to small customers and we also learned that price was king," said Frederick Abrew, president of Equitable Resources Inc, an LDC running its own pilot in Pennsylvania.
Abrew said Equitable's program offered customers better rates and more competitive options, while the company gleaned new marketing skills and learned about flaws in its billing system.
But he questioned state efforts to deregulate.

"We would argue for setting a uniform national standard. If we allow unbundling to proceed on a state-by-state basis, we'll end up with 1,500 different markets," he said, referring to the rough number of public utilities across the country.
Regardless of whether federal or state governments set the pace for deregulation, it seems clear that some companies and customers willing to meet change head on will benefit.

"We see unbundling as an inevitable future for the utility industry. Electric utilities will be required to offer customer choice by November 1, 1998, and there will be significant advantages for us to be there along with them," Bay State's Singer said.
